subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO END RELIEF ON JUNE 15
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the agreement under
which contributions were made by the federal government to the provinces of Canada to assist them in providing direct relief and other employment came to an end according to its terms on the 31st day of March last. This government advised the various provinces at that time that we would continue to make contributions for direct relief where it seemed that the provinces had an acute situation, that the need was great, and the provinces concerned, with their municipalities, were unable to cope with it. We said we would continue it until the end of May; expressing the hope, of course, that with improved conditions direct relief could soon be abandoned. There are many places in Canada, I am sure hon. members will be pleased to know, where assistance by direct relief has now been found1 not to be necessary.
Following up the first message to the provinces a further extension of dominion contribution was intimated, to carry forward to the 15th of this month. Perhaps there will be places in Canada where, by reason of exceptional circumstances, special consideration will have to be given by way of assistance, but at the same time there is no doubt that the pressure with respect to contributions to direct relief is diminishing in a very satisfactory manner. The intimation given to the provinces as to its discontinuance was founded upon information supplied to the Department of Labour, and on a review of the position of the various provinces with respect to their ability to take care of what direct relief was necessary during the coming summer.
I do not know that I can add anything further to what I have said, but I feel quite hopeful that during the summer months at least we shall find that in the majority of places throughout the dominion direct relief can be abandoned in view of the revival of activity in the building and other trades. However, the situation will be constantly under review by myself and the government, and if it appears that assistance is necessary it will be given very serious consideration.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS

speechtext:
Hon. ROBERT WEIR (Minister of Agriculture) moved the third reading of Bill No. 51, to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provisions in connection therewith.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before the third reading passes I should like to make a very few observations in connection with the bill. I believe all hon. members who have given any concern or thought during the past few years to the marketing of the primary products of the dominion, whether they be producers, those engaged in the marketing of the
3664	COMMONS
Marketing Act-Mr. Weir (Meljort)
products or those who consume the products, agree that there has been felt a need for some legislation or action which would tend to reduce to a minimum the wastage which now exists in our more or less haphazard method of marketing, and also that steps should be taken as far as possible to stabilize the prices of products of the primary producers.
In endeavouring to give effect to this desire or much felt need, we set out to prepare a bill which for some weeks has been under discussion both in the house and in committee of the whole house. In the preparation of it we gave careful study, first, to other marketing bills which have been passed and have been in force in various countries. However, after careful examination of these bills and the boards set up by such legislation we felt that the conditions with which they were formed to deal were so different from those confronting us in connection with the marketing and regulation of marketing of the primary products of Canada, that they could be of little use to us, certainly could not be adopted as a model, and could be used only as a guide here and there in the preparation of our bill.
It was therefore decided that we must first have clearly before us the conditions we wished to remedy in order to prepare a bill peculiarly suitable and adaptable to the conditions in Canada with which it had to deal. In the preparation of the bill we had numerous discussions with cooperative associations, private individuals engaged in primary production, and with the trade. In the first draft of the bill we had made it much more definite, dealing to a greater extent with specific commodities. But as other problems were presented it was felt that the very definiteness of it, limiting it to particular problems, made it inapplicable to the marketing of other products. Therefore the bill underwent a gradual change, becoming more comprehensive and, as one hon. member stated in discussion, became more in the nature of a skeleton of a bill which could be filled in and could better meet the varying conditions. This was also necessary so that every possibility of full cooperation between the provinces and the dominion could be brought about.
The fundamental principles of the bill as submitted to the house are briefly these: First, as far as was possible and as far as Was indicated by organizations of primary producers to place in their own hands the marketing of their own products. Secondly, in case of emergency or in dealing with a

primary product concerning which, due to geographical and other reasons it was difficult for the producers to organize, where it was felt by the government that some assistance or organization should be arranged, power is given the government to deal with such emergency or condition on its merits.
Then, in the third place, power is given in the bill to investigate spreads, or the cost of marketing, thereby giving an assurance to the producers that they will not be exploited in the marketing of their product, an assurance which applies similarly to the purchaser of such products. Then, power was given in the bill to deal with the importation and exportation of natural or primary products into and out of the dominion, so that under the different conditions in which we find ourselves we would have the machinery to enable us to take our place among the trading nations of the world.
Then, lastly, provision is made in the bill to enable complete cooperation between the provincial bodies to be set up and the federal bodies which may be set up. I give this brief review for this reason: It was no surprise when the bill was up for discussion that many hon. members should have traversed the very paths which we pursued in the preparation of the bill. They had in mind some specific commodities with which they wanted the bill to deal. However, although realizing that if the measure were so defined it would become ineffective as regards other commodities, yet as the amendments proposed did not in any way affect what we felt we had already set out in the bill and for which we had made definite provision and to set at rest the doubts of some persons, we accepted amendments to the bill based on the requests and desires of hon. members as evidenced in the discussion.
I believe therefore that it would be of interest to the house if I were to put on record a short analysis of the effect of the amendments to the bill as first brought down, to *bear out the statement I have made as to why the amendments were introduced and accepted.
1.	Principle
The fundamental principle embodied in this bill is that of governmental sanction and support of regulated marketing by producers and ether persons engaged in such activity, supplemented by direct governmental action when unusual conditions warrant such procedure. The amendments have in no way altered this principle.

Marketing Act-Mr. Weir (Melfort)
2.	Purpose
To regulate rather than to disrupt trade is the purpose of this bill. Improvement of conditions by the control or direction of marketing as to time, place, quantity, quality and manner of distribution was sought in the original bill. Regulation, with a minimum of interference with trade practices, is the keynote of this legislation. The amendments have in no way altered these objectives.
3.	Machinery of regulation
The machinery provided for in the bill consists of a central board appointed by the government and local boards created by persons engaged in production and/or marketing to which power to regulate the marketing of the natural product may be given. No change has been made in this connection by the amendments.
4.	Powers
The powers to be conferred upon the dominion board and by delegation upon local boards, namely, to regulate marketing, to raise funds, to compensate for loss under stated conditions, to require information, to cooperate with provincial boards, to register and license producers and persons engaged in marketing, remain almost exactly as they were in the bill as introduced. Clarifications having to do with pooling and collection of funds have been made and an extension of powers under clause (e), subsection (1), section 4, to include "processing" was made.
5.	Federal and provincial jurisdiction
Certain changes to clarify the intention and
make more certain the division of authority between the dominion and provincial bodies has been made but the purpose in this respect has in no way been changed.
6.	Regulation of import and export
This section of the original bill was redrafted and the provision re imposition of penalties, which in a measure conflicted with other similar provisions of the act, was deleted. However, the purpose of the section, namely, control of import and export trade in natural products within certain limitations remains as it was.
7.	Spreads
A number of changes have been made in the second part of the bill and several sections have been added. These are, for the most part, designed to establish more definitely the legal procedure in the case of prosecutions. There is no change in the principle or purpose of this part of the act.
8.	Summary of changes
There are ninety-two numbered or lettered sections, subsections, clauses or other divisions in the original bill. Of these thirty-three were altered in some respect by amendments but thirteen of these changes were of one or two words. The introduction of the word "natural" in the second part involved changes in eight sections or subsections.
9.	The introduction of provisions designed to clarify several sections involving such matters as "pooling" and the provision and use of "funds" by local boards each required changes in several other sections. In each of such instances it is believed the power to do the thing desired was conveyed in the original draft but to satisfy some who held doubts on the subject, amendments were agreed to.
The principal changes made are those affecting the definition of natural product, section 2 (e); limiting the demands upon the consolidated revenue fund, section 3 (9); removing uncertainty as to the use of funds collected, section 4 (4); defining the powers under section 9; improving the section having to do with import and export restrictions.
In moving the third reading of this bill, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I frankly requested constructive criticism of the bill as introduced, and I regret that the discussion so repeatedly went very far afield from the subject matter of the bill itself. I feel, however, that that may be due perhaps to the bill covering a new field. I regret that we have not had more constructive criticism but I sincerely wish to express my appreciation to those who have contributed to bringing the bill into the form in which it is at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can imagine hearing some of the hon. members weary of this heat remarking, "Could we not cut out this talkfest and have a vote and be through with it," but the minister himself evidently did not think that was the way to proceed, and I am only following his example in making a few remarks.

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
This is the government's first marketing baby, and like all events of that nature they have had great anguish over delivering the baby, so much so that they might very well have resorted to that ameliorating practice known as twilight sleep. But that might have injured the baby, and we do not want to do that. I certainly do not want to do that, and I am glad that the ministry staggered through with it the way they did eventually and got on to their feet somehow. But, Mr. Speaker, it was a most distressing spectacle. However, the baby has arrived, and with a good deal of the Tory plumage all gone, but there are some objectionable features the size of one's fist still sticking out all over it. But there is just enough for identification purposes, just enough to show its semi-Tory origin, or its foster parentage, because the government was not the real parent of the bill at all. This bill was born of the farmers and producers, of western Canada particularly, and especially of the Pacific coast. That is where it came from, and the statement that the government is thrusting this upon the people is not right. It is the growers that are thrusting this marketing bill down the throats of an unwilling government, except the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir, Melfort) who was ready for it for some time past. That is the real position.
My analysis of this bill is quite different from the minister's. He regretted that there were not more constructive criticisms. Why, Mr. Speaker, so constructive have our criticisms been that this is almost a new bill entirely. According to my count there have been twenty-nine amendments, and I could make it a little more if I desired to stretch it. I could bring it to thirty-three, or thirty-five or even forty, but I have not counted those small amendments to which the minister referred. In order to leave no doubt about it I am going to, take the necessary time out of my precious forty minutes to outline the changes that have been made in this bill and, Mr. Speaker, I hope you will give me three minutes' notice of the expiry of my forty minutes because I do not even know what time it was when I started.
I have classified the changes into three divisions, "very important" changes, "less important" changes, and "unimportant" changes. I shall not have time to go over them all, but I shall refer to them.
First, section 2, paragraph (e) extends the definition of natural product to include lumber and food and drink derived from products of forest, lake, sea and river. I think this

new list of natural products is much better than the original definition, perhaps because it is almost identical with what I suggested myself if hon. gentlemen will recall my remarks on the second reading of the bill.
The next amendment deals with section 3, subsection 9, and provides that instead of permitting the costs of the board to be paid from consolidated revenue fund, they shall be appropriated by parliament. My right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) urged that amendment very strongly.
The next deals with section 4, subsection 1, paragraph (a) and provides for the setting up of a single selling agency which may be designated. Without this there is no centralized selling possible. That amendment was insisted upon by the producers. It was put in once by the ministry but they could hardly find it and they had to put it in the second time.
The fourth amendment deals with section 4, subsection 1, paragraph (c) and provides for the pooling of proceeds received from the sale of a product. No such provision existed in the original act. The minister tried to persuade us that it was there but nobody could find it, not even himself. There again, they had to insert it twice before it was really there.
Amendment number 5 deals with section 4, subsection 1, paragraph (e) and enables grants or loans to be made for the assistance of processing farm products. I do not want to plume myself too much, but that was my suggestion. I should like to refer for a moment to what this means as I believe it has a significance far beyond the conception of most hon. members. I gave an illustration of what "processing" could mean by referring to experimental or demonstration abattoirs which could be set up under these grants or loans. It is only by this means that we can have a satisfactory solution of the question of abattoirs and live stock marketing generally. This matter has been in my mind for years and I have always advocated it. The time has now come to close in on it. It provides also for the establishment of cheese and butter factories such as they have in other countries with which we have to compete. They have them in Denmark, in the United States, in Australia and in New Zealand. Fine large plants are established in those countries to which the producer can take his milk and be paid immediately on the basis of the butter fat content. This provides for the assistance to the processing of the fifteen or twenty dairy commodities that are made out of milk. It

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
provides also for the processing of fruits, vegetables, wool, maple products, of wheat into flour, of oats into meal and many other forms of processing. All these activities are covered by the single word "processing." I have not the time to dwell at length upon the scope of this amendment or to show how far embracing it is.
The sixth amendment deals with section 4, subsection 2, and limits the powers which the dominion board may delegate to a local board to those contained in section 4. This prevents a local board from getting money from parliament to pay the costs of operation or to enable them to compensate for loss. It also prevents the dominion board from delegating to a local board the right given to it under section 9 actually to sell commodities. I remember quite distinctly that my right hon. leader spoke very strongly against what was embodied in the original bill and this has been amended.
Amendment 7 deals with section 4, subsections 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8. These are all entirely new and they provide for obtaining funds from producers instead of from parliament, which funds are to be used to pay any loss, compensation to producers, equalized payments, that is, pool receipts and building up reserves. According to the original bill, these expenses were to be borne by the state, but this amendment was finally inserted at the request of the growers.
Amendment number 8 deals with section 5, subsection 3 and enables the minister to demand a poll before a scheme is approved. The original bill made no provision for a poll. I am sure the government included this amendment because of the discussion which took place. The minister was good enough to invite suggestions.
Amendment number 9 deals with section 7, subsection 4, and provides that if a poll is taken and a scheme adopted, it cannot be revoked without a further poll being taken of the growers. The original bill contained no provision for a poll before revocation.
Amendment number 10 deals with section 9. This gives the dominion board power to set up a scheme itself and, as amended, it makes it clear that the scheme so set up may permit the board either to regulate marketing or actually to sell a commodity. The local boards are not allowed to do this. It also makes it clear that in setting up such schemes they can only relate to interprovincial and export trade. This very important amendment was suggested by the Liberal opposition.
Amendment number 11 deals with section 15. This is an entirely new section and
provides that the dominion board must make an annual report to the minister which report must be laid before parliament within a stated period of time. I have a very vivid recollection of my right hon. leader suggesting this amendment.
Amendment number 12 deals with section 16, paragraph (b), and extends the scope of the investigations to include investigations in natural products as well as in regulated products. I am not quite sure as to who suggested this amendment but I think it was someone on this side. If it were not, it was the producers themselves.
Amendment number 13 deals with section 20 and makes the committee's findings merely a report to the minister rather than a determination for which penalties could be imposed.
These are the thirteen amendments which I consider to be " very important." That may be considered an unlucky number but as one amendment takes in seven subsections, the total is really more than thirteen, really seventeen.
We come now to the "less important" amendments. Amendment number 14 deals with section 4, subsection 1, paragraph (c) and provides that no compensation can be given for loss if the grade is unsuitable for market or is incurred as a result of agreements with foreign countries. Had this amendment not been included the government would have been exploited in all directions. Had the bill as originally drafted been passed this marketing act would never have got started. It would have been like the British act of 1931, simply a negation on the statute books. That was what happened with the British act until it was amended once and again two years later.
Amendment 15 deals with section 4, subsection 1, paragraph (i). This paragraph originally gave the local board the power to hold real property but it has since been deleted.
Amendment number 16 deals with section 12 and makes it necessary that the governor in council rather than the minister license importers and exporters. The clause by which the governor in council could provide penalties for any breach in connection with this section has been deleted.
Amendment number 17 deals with section
23.	This is an entirely new section and provides for the transmitting of reports of investigating committees to the provincial attorneys general for such action as is deemed necessary. The next amendment, number 18, deals with section 24. This is a new section and provides that the accused in any action as above may demand trial by jury. Amend-

ment number 19 deals with section 25 and provides that the minister must file annually with parliament a report oi all proceedings taken under the investigating sections. This is entirely new. Amendment number 20 deals with section 26. This is a new section which declares that if any section of the act is found to be beyond the powers of parliament, it shall not affect the remaining provisions thereof. This is one of the very few amendments proposed by the government itself.
With the "less important" and "unimportant" amendments, there are 29 in all. I think it should be noted that not one single amendment has been suggested by what we know as the C.'C.F'ers. They were in favour of the bill just as it was brought down. I do not include the United Farmers of Alberta when I refer to the C.C.F'ers because they, the former, have renounced them. This is an example of the delightful harmony we find between the different portions of the far C.C.F. corner. They can dispense hot air by the barrel full but when it comes to helping the government to improve this bill, of which they said they approved, the results have been nil. Perhaps I should exempt the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man). That hon. gentleman says he is not a member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and he has made a valuable suggestion in connection with this bill, but I do not know whether he made it before I did or not.
There are one or two other members who made suggestions with regard to organization grants. The government of which I was a member made the first valuable contribution by way of an organization grant to the Cooperative Live Stock Marketing Association. The first year in 1928 this grant was $5,000; the second year, it was $10,000, and the third year it was $20,000. This splendid live stock cooperation agency went along fine until 1931, when the present government deliberately killed that institution by withholding the grant when Great Britain went off the gold standard. With the loss on the pound sterling and with no grant this great institution was simply stricken amidships and went down under the blow. If some hon. member referred to this question of organization grants before your humble servant did, the fact remains that the government of which I had the honour to be a member, was the first to act upon this policy away back in 1928.
As much as I would like to follow all these amendments up to the last I have not the time, so I will mention the twenty-ninth and

if nobody objects I would like to give the intervening ones to Hansard.

I think my right hon. leader had something to do with that too. It may surprise some hon. members if this marketing act should not be and indeed was preceded by another act, a very necessary prerequisite to this marketing bill. I will not ask the house to accept my statement on that; I will refer to Major Elliot, Minister of Agriculture for Great Britain. I have no doubt my good friend the minister expects some day when this bill goes through to be the minister of agriculture in Canada representing the same position that Major Elliot represents in Great Britain namely, that he is the pioneer in Canada of the idea of quotas, turning on the tap for larger or smaller quotas according to the requirements of the occasion. I do not, however, know about that; I do not want to see anybody play the DeValera for Canada in our relationship to Great Britain, and that is what I am afraid will be the result. Let me read what Major Elliot says about the prerequisites to a marketing act:
Agriculture, at home and abroad, is recognizing the urgent need for an improved marketing technique and is setting out in diverse ways to obtain it.

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
In two main directions is reform being pursued-in the direction of standardization and in that of organization, the latter in order not merely to implement the former but to enable producers, by a combination of their man-power and, if they so desire, of their produce-power and their money-power, to control effectively the marketing end of their business and enjoy equal opportunity with other highly organized groups in the industrial community.
Major Elliot divides this into two distinct subdivisions: standardization of product and then the marketing thereof. Surely it is within the memory of almost every hon. member that for eight and a half years the Liberal government, headed by my right hon. leader, spent a great deal of their time in standardization of farm products from one end of Canada to the other. That is the great prerequisite to a marketing proposal. During that period where were hon. gentlemen opposite? Their most effective harpooner, the then leader of the opposition, was looking for my short ribs half of the time. Where were the birds to my left who are presumed to represent agriculture? They were in the same category for the first four years; after that they came to the conclusion that maybe this was all right and many of them so signified. But some of my best measures were left on the order paper to die there because I could not get the support of those who were then in opposition either official or unofficial, or a sufficient number on any side. One of those measures was the Hay and Straw Act which in 1929 fell thus by the wayside, which some two years ago I had the pleasure of assisting my hon. friend to put through.
Major Elliot continues:
Standardization is a fundamental principle of our modern commercial system.
So this foundation upon which this marketing bill is built, was laid by the former Liberal government. I am taking, not my definition but that of Major Elliot of the close relationship between standardization and marketing. Let me read another paragraph of what he says:
The commercial advantages of standardization are well known and need not be repeated here. In this country, as elsewhere, legislation has proved to be necessary to put the standardization of farm produce on a national basis. Here, it has taken the form of the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marketing) Acts, 1928 and 1931.
We were almost through with our grading and standardizing policy under the preceding Liberal government by the time Great Britain started; we were a lap ahead of even the mother country in the standardization of farm
products, as over there they are only now at some of that work.
Now comes the marketing bill. Because my hon. friends opposite through this bill build upon our Liberal foundation, am I going to refuse to accept it in accordance with the stand I took on the second reading? I am not going to proclaim exactly at this stage how I am going to vote on the third reading division, if I can avoid doing so. But I will try to present the facts. The measure was such a Tory distortion of Liberal principles and so contrary to what the farmers asked for that one could easily take one side or the other and yet justify one's position. Major Elliot continues:
So the time has come to develop further the policy to which successive governments have already contributed and prepare to rebuild the whole organizational structure of our agricultural marketing.
He points out that the first prerequisite was to get standardization. I will leave it to the house and to the country whether the Liberal government have not done that. Consequently, with all these amendments made to this measure largely at the instance of the Liberal opposition and the producers, we have given to the country the first prerequisite of a marketing act. I can and I do claim that the first principle of this bill as now amended, defaced as it is by some Tory distortions that have been thrown in, is now, built upon Liberal foundations already cited, and is really Liberal if such few distortions were eliminated. That is what it is, even after these amendments have been made, but some of the distortions, the Tory excrescences that I abominate, are still there. What shall I do in an emergency of that nature? Heaven help me that I may make the right choice, because it is not an easy one. This report to the Minister of Agriculture which I hold in my hand, and which I will read will confirm my statement. One is on pretty strong grounds when one reads something from official reports as I have been doing and propose to do. This is the report of Doctor J. F. Booth, commissioner of farm economics, to his minister, the Minister of Agriculture. On page 222 thereof, I find under the subhead of "Farmers' Business Organizations" the following. I hope the house will bear with me because this is very important and if it means anything, it means-well, that it is favourable to this bill. But coming as it does from this intermediary Tory source, one can
3670	COMMONS
Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
come to another conclusion if one wants to. It reads:
Records and statistics properly tabulated and summarized form the basis for investigation and comparative analysis in economic research. From a national standpoint Canada is without this ground work for a study of farmers' business organizations. It is true that considerable work has been accomplished by provincial and federal bodies in collecting and presenting facts on cooperative organizations in Canada. The information available, however, does not present us with a complete picture of business organization among farmers throughout the dominion or permit of research and analysis which it is generally agreed should be undertaken. At the time the branch was instituted-
That was about 1928.
-it was understood that cooperative marketing would receive consideration. With this in view plans were made to obtain the basic information necessary to a comprehensive program of research and service.
Next comes a paragraph that I would rather skip, but I can read it if anybody thinks I am garbling the report. He goes on:
With the assistance of provincial registrars and' from various other sources a list of farmers' business organizations in Canada has been prepared. On this list there is a total of 1,759 associations. In response to a first request for information 737 or 42 per cent of the solicited organizations replied. This has been followed up by a second request in some provinces and where necessary the associations will be circularized a third time.
In the study of farmers' business organizations special attention will be given to financial analysis. If such organizations are going to develop and endure they must withstand scrutiny of the same nature as private business. Certain tests well known in business practice are applied. Other problems to which the branch is giving attention are uniformity in financial statements, type and method of organization, raising of funds, credit operations. A central bureau of records of this kind will permit a study of business practices which include financing, price and sales policies and advertising. The scope of this work naturally extends to the operations of marketing agencies and distribution costs. Legal phases, membership and contractual relations present problems, all of which have a bearing on the development of farmers' business organizations, local or national in character. Continuity of work over a period of years and especially covering this period of economic stress should be significant and of considerable historical value.
In addition to the survey of farmers' business organizations the branch is endeavouring to obtain a complete and up-to-date record of all other agricultural organizations. A listing of this nature will include the non-commercial organizations such as fruit growers and live stock improvement associations. The index compiled at the present time contains over 400 societies with names of officers, membership affiliations and other information. When the records for the dominion as a whole are com-
pleted and the bureau becomes fully established the branch will provide a directory and may be in position to act as a consulting agency for farmers' organizations and those interested in their development.
That is what the Liberal government of that day had in mind in establishing the economic branch, so that it would be a centre, a directory, a registration and advisory retreat to which all such organizations as this could rally from one end of Canada to the other. It is said that Doctor Booth is slated to be one of the central board. If that be so, then he will act in a double capacity, he will be head of the economic branch and a member of the board, and will have a double opportunity of tying up voluntarily this great organization from one end of Canada to the other in one centre. I can imagine the valuable advice that such a board or directory could have given in years past when great farm movements, economic and educational, were wrecked one after another by going into politics. We saw the old Grangers, that came from the United States in the early 70's, twenty years afterwards totally wrecked on the rocks of commerce mixed with politics. Look at the same movement of which I had the honour to be the first president in 1901, that started out as an educational body, non-political and non-commercial; it stayed that way for five years, and then in 1919 gravitated into politics. The itch for power, the thirst for this kind of adventure was strong, and after certain years of successful service they wanted to get into politics, against which, of course, there is no law. Politics and commerce, however, do not seem to work together, they never have. I wish I had time to read some of the platform of the old Grange movement that started out so nobly and ended so disastrously in the form of the Patrons of Industry twenty years afterwards.
I can count more than one movement of the same kind. In the case of the one I know so well, the old Grain Growers' Association, as long as your humble servant was president and Hon. R. S. Lake vice-president both politics and commerce of a purchasing nature were kept out. But the day came when some arose "who knew not Joseph," and that great farmers' organization drifted into the same evil that had wrecked the Patrons of Industry, nearly thirty years previously. Of course, they have the right to do it if they want to, but we cannot keep up our commercial end successfully if we are jumping into the political end at the same time. We are in danger of that at this very minute. If that is the desirable thing, why should the C.C.F. support this bill, as it is neither state

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
socialism, or production for use and not for profit? We have therefore a rallying centre in the capital; we the former Liberal government established it ourselves in the economic branch to make it a source of advice for all who would seek it on any phase whatever of their activities. If we had had access to the central board or the economic branch through all the past years do you think that such racketeers as Aaron Shapiro could have paralyzed and bedevilled the cooperative agricultural activities of this country and this continent as he did? He could not. But farmers in their difficulties and distress will sometimes listen to the wiles of the devil himself.

speechtext:
When people are
in trouble and anyone throws them any kind of life-line they grab at it. Shapiro was the quintessence of hypocrisy, delusion and racketeering. Who was going to advise these newly organized units as long as they were spread abroad on the face of the earth with no centre to converge on? They had such a centre under our Liberal government in the economic branch as I have just referred to. That is one of the reasons why I take the ground that I have taken with respect to this bill. It may be asked, Why did we not start a marketing board? We were fighting a sister dominion-Australia-because they were shooting the objectionable phases of a marketing board onto Canada under the "Patterson" plan. We did not believe in passing on those objectionable phases to the mother country, at that time at all events. We gave evidence of our desire to promote marketing proposals by starting up the Cooperative Live Stock Producers in the manner I have described, a first class commission organization at first and then an equally first class export organization until the casualty that occurred to it because of the gross neglect of this government.
Now I might say more. I think I have ten minutes yet. I should like to devote a little of that time to my hon. friends on my left, the C.C.F'ers. It is a strange thing that on the second reading of this bill I found myself in company with these birds over here. Well, you cannot always choose your associates. If I think a thing is right I have to stand by it; I am not going to run away because someone else also thinks it is right. I was thinking of the ghastly company that I was in, a most excruciating experience from both directions. But, Mr. Speaker, I have recently been looking over the history of reforms, and
this is a reform bill but in bad company. It is in the hands of foster parents, I admit, and they naturally make a mess of it. But what was the history of reform bills in the early part of last century, who finally had to espouse them, after opposing them to the uttermost at the beginning? What about Tory Peel? What about Tory Disraeli? They stayed Tories but they took up the Liberal program embodied in the reform bills and free trade. Was it not so with Gladstone also, only he remained Liberal. Bright and Cobden undoubtedly were the authors of free trade, but the previous Tory, Gladstone came over and supported it, because it grew so popular. The last straw that turned the tide was the potato famine in Ireland, a small thing in a way but terrible in Ireland, but it helped to concentrate and crystallize public sentiment and bring about free trade. So here we have our friends on the other side performing the same stunt as Peel and Disraeli, just walking off with the other fellow's clothes. They still fit me in some particulars. I want some of the distortions taken out, some more of the Tory plumage taken off if possible. But my C.C J. hon. friends over here are full of an abundance of hot air and heifer dust; that is about all they deal in, not having contributed one iota for the benefit of this bill, and their leader is parading around the country asking the people to flock to his standard. We have bhe Coldwells in Saskatchewan, the Philpotts and the whatnots in Ontario. What are they doing? Just shooting hot air with not one practical idea behind it. Here in amending this bill, they were given an opportunity to display some of their knowledge and ability, to do something but talk, but they failed utterly.
I seem to have covered quite a bit of ground, but there is one thing more. On the second reading unfortunately I had to vote differently from nearly all of my party, but I do not consider that there was anything contradictory as between my attitude and that of my leader. The duty of a leader is to have a much wider vision than that of a humble follower. The duty of a leader as I see it is not only to represent one great occupation but to represent all occupations in Canada, producers and consumers. There is absolutely no recognition of consumers in this bill. The duty of a leader is not only to represent all Canada and all businesses and occupations in Canada but to recognize the rights and interests of all the units of the British commonwealth and the relationships of Canada, especially commercial, with the rest of the world. That is the attitude that

Marketing Act-Mr. Motherwell
must be taken by the great leader of a great party, and I would not have my right hon. leader take any other position. On the other hand the scope of my duty as I see it, is relatively circumscribed. I represent a rural constituency. I do not say that I always consult them; I have to assume that they expect me to do my duty as I see it and explain to them later. When you are two thousand miles away you cannot rush to your constituency for this, that or the other thing; it takes us all our time to understand what we are discussing here, without trying to impart it to others at every stage of development. By virtue of my position in the preceding government, however, I am compelled to consider the producers and farmers generally, the growers as we call them on the Pacific, if there is any preference to be given to anyone. I gladly do that, though I hope I am broad enough to recognize the principle that you cannot do full justice to the producers without giving fair consideration to the consumers as well, and that has been my position. There is nothing contradictory or incompatible in a leader expressing a different position from that of a humble follower. Those positions are entirely different, as I have stated. I make these remarks in reference to the second reading of this bill, in reply to one or two letters I have received expressing regret that I could not maintain the entity of the party and vote against the second reading of the bill.
I think this is a sufficiently important occasion to speak for my full forty minutes, but just to show that I am not unnecessarily taking up time I will conclude by saying that I do not intend to make any pronouncement as to the way I will vote either on any possible amendment or on the third reading of the bill. I do not know whether in my desire not to do so or in my anxiety to show my interest in the whole matter I may have crossed my wires and already revealed how I am going to vote, but if I have done so you will understand the reason. I have decided to reserve my decision until the actual vote is taken, whether it be on an amendment or otherwise. I only decided that at the very last moment; my few notes were based upon another assumption to be revealed later.

Mr. Speaker, after the storms in committee and the various discords passed away I had the feeling that the third reading might be an occasion of harmony and amity, on which the whole house might get together to advise the farmers of this country to make the best of an act which affords them some opportunity. (Mr. Motherwell.]
Because of that feeling I shall not traverse at any length the ground covered by the last speaker, the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), nor shall I enter into a discussion of the relative attitudes of those in this corner of the house and those whom he represents in relation to this bill. As to the attitude of those in this corner, including myself, I think I shall leave it to Hansard, to this house and to the farmers of this country to decide as to whether we do not occupy a reasonably fair position in respect to our attitude, in the contributions we may have made, in our understanding of the problems and of the bill itself, as compared with my hon. friends to my right. I sympathized with the ex-Minister of Agriculture when he was reluctantly forced to associate himself with us for once in supporting a measure brought in by a Conservative government. I think perhaps if any argument were required, that is the last and final argument in favour of this bill. It shows that even he, driven between two contrary winds and tides, was forced by his own knowledge of the situation and his own inherent sympathy for the farmer to support that which, as he said, he felt was a move in the right direction, even though in doing so he had to associate with those whom I have mentioned.

speechtext:
I merely point out that the association to which I belong, which the minister was so careful to mention, has joined the other association to which he has referred.
I,	of course, was elfected as a United Farmers of Alberta member, and I am subject to the action taken by that association. However, that is mostly by the way. I had no intention of entering into any competition, nor indeed bad I any intention of referring to hot air, though in passing I might remark that a perusal of the pages of Hansard might induce some people, even those who have not had the pleasure of sitting in this house during part of the debate, to believe that all the hot air that came from this side of the house was not confined to the southeast corner.
This bill has been described and may be looked upon as a radical departure from

Marketing Act-Mr. Speakman
customary methods. In some respects that is so, but I agree with the ex-Minister of Agriculture that it follows in logical sequence the actions taken in prior years and by former ministers, and may I say in particular by the ex-Minister of Agriculture for whom, in spite of some of his strictures, I entertain the highest regard as having been one of the best ministers of agriculture this country has seen. To my mind there were three definite stages through which to pass, three definite steps to be taken in sequence, and to have taken a step like this before the other two steps had been taken, before the foundation had been laid, would have been impossible. The first step, of course, was the work carried on by the different departments of agriculture and by various farm bodies through experimental farms, through research, through education and so on, to improve the quality and kind of the various farm products. Obviously it is useless to establish a marketing act un-les you have a suitable type of product to market. Then followed that long sequence of inspection and grading acts which have not only graded, divided and regulated the products themselves but have accustomed the farmers to inspection, regulation, grading and control, and have disabused their minds of that impression perhaps formerly held, that any individual can of his own volition and without regard to marketing conditions and to his fellowmen produce just exactly that class and kind of stuff which he himself would like to produce. They have learned that they must, for their own good and for the common good, defer to law and as I say, subject themselves, to regulation, inspection and control of all kinds. Had it not been for that they would not now be ready to accept the bill before the house. I say at this point that while this is a new step and a most important step, it would be impossible were it not for the work done in former years by former ministers. It is a combination of that work,- the most important, but unable to stand by itself.
Now, as we come to the bill itself as amended may I express my pleasure and gratification concerning certain of the amendments which have been made. I believe I have studied the bill as carefully as any other private member, and I am unable to see that in essence the main principles of the bill have been affected. What has been done is to clarify many points suggested, but suggested in so vague a manner as to be capable of complete misapprehension and complete misinterpretation. I refer to such matters as the ability and right of the producers organizations to carry on pooling projects. I think that would have been embraced in the presentation of a scheme, but for their satisfaction and to place the matter beyond doubt I believe it was necessary that the conditions should be placed clearly and specifically in the bill. Then, I might mention others,-the ability of the board to designate the agency through which the marketing might be carried on. This again is made clear beyond doubt, that if the producers have formed their pools and wish to operate through such pools as their agencies, such agencies may be designated as the agencies through which marketing shall be carried on. And so it leaves the way clearly open for each producers' organization to organize so as to market and to handle its own affairs in the way it deems best and which experience has taught it to be wisest.
The bill itself is, of course, stringent-and to my mind it must be so. In my view one of the most fatal mistakes in a bill of this kind would have been to endow the board in the first instance with too narrow powers, and to restrict it in its operations. We are entering a new field, a field where new problems will be encountered, some of which are unforeseen at the present time. It is a field which will be subject to the changing conditions not only in this but in other countries, and to my mind it is essential for the success of the bill, the success of the board and the success of the whole program that from the commencement the board shall be endowed with sufficient powers, wide and strong, to meet those eventualities as they may arise. I am glad to see that this has been done, and that the legislation does and will include within its scope almost any essential action which must be taken to relieve the situation now existing among the producers of Canada.
There are points in the bill to which, under ordinary circumstances and had we been living in a world as it was in former years, I should have taken strong exception. For instance, I should have taken exception to the powers to control exports and imports. But as I look around the world to-day and as we all look around the world to-day and note the actual conditions which exist and which apparently will exist for years to come I find I cannot take that exception, because once the nations of the world have launched themselves upon that course of attempted selfsufficiency, no matter how unsuitable the climate or conditions-once	they have
launched themselves upon that course it will take years before they can possibly retrace their steps. In the world in which we must

Marketing Act-Mr. Speakman
live, a world which has been described to us by a man of great experience as one in which Great Britain remains the one country offering reasonable opportunity for the sale of our farm products in a world where tariffs have become the least part of restriction, and where absolute prohibition, licensing of imports and the most strict application of the quota system is applied in almost every one of the great European countries which at one time had relatively open markets-in this world we must realize forcibly that through this board we must have the power to regulate and absolutely to control the export of goods in order that we may meet existing conditions.
The condition as regards imports may not be as obvious, but may I point this out to hon. gentlemen. Assuming that the bill does all that we hope it will do; assuming that we succeed in the coming years in raising prices to a reasonable level-I am not speaking about exorbitant prices, but I am referring to stabilizing prices and freeing them from those seasonal and most calamitous price fluctuations and thereby establishing the farmer upon a reasonable and suitable basis-what will be the result? The result will be that during times when the outside world market is at a lower level than our own market we will be subjected to a flooding into this country of those similar goods from other countries seeking markets, countries the goods of which had been debarred from other markets and who see in Canada the Eldorado of their dreams. Having taken these steps and having undergone such sacrifice in arranging our own price level, would it be possible for us to leave our market completely open to be shattered and brought to naught at any time by the importations from other countries? To my mind it is essential, if eventually we are to succeed, that there must be some provision whereby we may stop those importations at times when they would demoralize and break our own markets.
It is not for the good of the consumer that the producer of this country should be put out of business. That is one point I should like to impress upon those hon. gentlemen whose chief concern-and laudable concern-is for the consumers. They speak of restriction; they speak of the possibility of having scarcity instead of plenty. I say there is nothing which will more easily bring about potential and actual scarcity than to continue as we are, expecting the producers to bring forward their crops produced at a loss. They cannot and they will not continue in that way. It would be far better for the consumers to have a steady flow of products at 
reasonable prices and at prices which can be depended upon to be maintained from oDe year's end to another than to be subject to this overwhelming probability that some time or some day under conditions as they are, unless remedied, the producers may simply cease to produce. Under such conditions where would the consumer be? Then he would see soaring prices, and he would see real scarcity. To my mind in protecting the producers who, alone, constitute almost fifty per cent of the consumers, and in enabling them to organize, to stabilize, to regulate and to place their own business upon a sane and satisfactory basis, we are affording the best guarantee for the future prosperity and future welfare of the rest of Canada.
Because of these things, Mr. Speaker, I welcomed the bill at its inception. Along with others, I had visions of such a bill years ago; I know that the Minister of Agriculture had, and certainly many of us had. I regret that it took so long to work out the measure, to meet conditions and to introduce the bill. I should liked to have seen it working now. I realize that the bill cannot be perfect. As I said before, and as has been stated by many hon. members, we are venturing into that which for this country is a new field and a new venture. There is nothing in this world, save experience alone, which will teach us just where the rocks and quicksands may lie, which will teach us exactly what difficulties we may have to encounter, or which will teach us exactly what measures may have to be taken in order to meet those difficulties. So I do not expect this to be a perfect bill any more than I would expect a new-born child to go out and do a day's work in the ha3ffields. That requires development; the child must grow up. But I do say this, that in my opinion, and I am giving it for what it is worth, and in the opinion of almost every farmer in my province who has communicated with me upon the subject, this bill does afford a hope. It does provide the initial machinery. It does make it possible for us to go forward and improve in the doing. Because of these things I give this bill the same support on the third reading that I gave it on the second, that I gave it in committee and that I have given it at all times.
May I suggest this to the house? There are two essentials upon which the work to be done under this bill will absolutely depend for its success. First is the cooperation among the producers, the working together by the producers under the terms of this bill. I suggest to the house that if this bill affords some opportunity to the producers to do this

Marketing Act-Mr. Lapointe
thing, it is the duty of this house to encourage them to do so. That is one reason, Mr. Speaker, why I have always spoken and argued in its favour. I realize some of its weaknesses, but I realize too that unless we can give to the farmers who are to benefit from this measure some feeling of encouragement, some hope that the bill is worth while, some feeling that it affords them an opportunity, we could not expect it to succeed nor could it succeed. I would like to see the united opinion of this house behind this bill, but that seems impossible. I sincerely hope to see a reasonably united opinion among the farmers that they will make the best use possible of this measure which is here provided and of acts to a similar effect which have been or will be passed in the various provinces.
There is just one other thought, and with that I shall conclude. The success of this bill again will depend, as is the case with all other bills of this nature, upon its administration. You can have a good bill badly administered and it will come to nothing. You can have a bill that affords opportunities for good or ill, such as this bill does, and if it is properly administered by men with the right viewpoint it will succeed. So, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the two essentials are an understanding cooperation on the part of the farmers and a sympathetic and efficient administration by the boards. With those twm essentials present, I believe that this bill will start us in the proper way and enable us to say that something has been done, that an advancement has been made towards raising the lot of the producer to that level where we should like to see it.
No one imagines that this bill by itself is a cure-all. No one,would be so foolish. Personally I agree with those who feel that before we can have conditions as they should be we must deal radically-no matter who may not like that word-with the whole financial question and with the application of finance to our daily vocation. May I suggest this also, that supposing we have a financial system equal to the wildest dreams of the most extreme visionary, even then if you are to have parity between one class and another, if you are to have a system that will work fairly smoothly, you must have an organization of those classes that work. You must have organization of producers in an organized world, and action along the lines of this bill would be essential no matter under what system we worked. Because of these things, Mr. Speaker, I can only hope that the bill will be a success, that its objects will be achieved.
I express further the hope that every farmers' organization and every producer in the country will come together to do what they can do under the terms of this bill, no matter what weaknesses they may find in it, in order to improve their own lot.

Well, what is the difference? Of course the economic depression has made people suffer in such a tremendous way that many have become despondent and their normal resistance to measures which are arbitrary * and authoritarian seems to have weakened. But let me tell my hon. friend that this bill is not merely for an emergency situation. Let me say to the members of the house generally that this bill is going to be the law of Canada for all time to come unless and until it is repealed by parliament. It is not there at all as an emergency. We are making a leap in the dark. During this discussion many hon. members have described this measure as an experiment. Why make the experiment at the expense of the primary producer or the farmer? The great danger in bad times is to force the acceptance of poor remedies. Sometimes these remedies instead of curing the disease, make it worse. During the course of his remarks, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) referred to the dislocation which had taken place in agriculture and our economic life. If that dislocation is not helped by this measure, will he advocate more drastic remedies? Planned marketing is a theory, but farmers do not live on theories. I represent a constituency which is made up mostly of consumers, but although there is nothing in this bill to protect the consumer, I do not want to discuss it from a class viewpoint. tion did not decrease proportionately. We must admit that our whole fiscal system bears heavily against the farmer. He must bear the greater burden than he ought to be made to bear. Agriculture is a highly individualized occupation. It is an industry which is conducted on a smaller scale than any other. I see it is my hon. friends to my left who do not like my remarks. I am surprised at that. I will ask them to use their patience for a little while.
Of course the Russian communists went further than most of the planners in other countries. They abolished all private capitalism. They took charge of all imports 74726-233
and exports, hours of work, all conditions, everything exactly like conditions governing soldiers and sailors elsewhere. They organized a big planning unit in Russia, the head being at Moscow and extending to every remote part of the territory. They called it the All Union Planning Commission. They had a national planning commission at .Moscow, a planning commission in every one of the seven what they call constitutive republics of the soviet, and also one in every one of the thirty so-called autonomous republics of the union. Then there was one in every little section and territory but all welded into a big whole, working under the direction of the state. Under this system Russia has become a trading unit, and if the system is a success, Russia will be the greatest trading corporation in the world. Of course it shoots any peasants or old-fashioned people who do not believe in being planned in that way. Our own bill is a mere kindergarten compared with the planning of Russia. Here they satisfy themselves with misrepresenting those who oppose the bill.
In Italy a different method was adopted. There they did not do away altogether with private ownership, but they organized the state into many corporations, guilds, also all im-der a commission of their own and welded into a unit, the result being that at least part of the individual freedom of the subject is taken away.
In Germany the system is still in an immature state and cannot be fully appreciated and criticised. It is still subject to variation according to the whims of the restless chancellor. But one thing certain is that there is always an armed ipoliceman pretty near representing the chancellor and there to see that the planning is well done and observed by everybody. Sir Norman Angell, speaking of those various dictatorships, said that they represent the psychology of the lynching party. Whatever my friends to my left may think about my views these are things that I cannot swallow and that as a Liberal I shall never digest.
Last year it was my privilege to be invited to a debate held at Hart House by the debating society of the university of Toronto. It was being conducted under parliamentary rules; there was the government on one side and the opposition on the other. I was defending Liberalism along with two of the students of the university against three opponents. The debate was a very interesting one of course until I spoke, but one thing which I remember and which I thought was

Marketing Act-Mr. Lapointe

rather bold when it was stated at the time but which seems to me now rather reasonable, was this: of course in the university there is a strong element of those who do not recognize either the Liberal or the Conservative party as their affiliation; they are Fabians, Marxists, communists, C.C.F.'s and many other denominations. We did not know which way they would vote and the Conservative. debaters made an appeal to them, telling them that after all Tory policy and communist policy are both based upon the same theory, both based upon the interference of the state in the private business of the citizen. They offered along those lines a strong argument which I had some difficulty to repel successfully. We, however, won the day.

They were wrong when they were saying that, but I know my hon. friends will not say I am unfair when I state that they are more to the left than we are. They represent a more extreme left than we do. We are witnessing a union of the extreme right and the extreme left on this bill. It was noticeable during the speech of the hon. member for South Vancouver (Mr. Maclnnis); he was pleased to quote the words, many of them, of the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency (Mr. Dorion) and he said: That is our doctrine; that is exactly what we promulgated at our conference in Regina last year. Well, it will be for my hon. friend to try to extricate himself from this embrace. But coming back to the hon. member for South Vancouver, he said something to which I wish to allude. He said: "Hon. gentlemen to my right are speaking all the time of liberty and freedom, and it gives me a pain in the neck." Well, sir, I must tell my hon. friend that I am a Liberal, and I still believe in liberty and freedom, freedom of association, freedom of speech and freedom of exchange, even if it gives him a pain anywhere in his anatomy.
I want to refer to the stand taken by the Labour opposition in Great Britain as to the

marketing act of last year. Of course the word "planning" was borrowed by Mr. Elliot from Mr. Cole. They approved of the principle of the bill, and I am not surprised at that. But they moved an amendment that all lands should be nationalized, because they said that it is the logical conclusion.

It is only piecemeal planning that you are doing; their stand was for the nationalization of the land. I shall quote from an article of the Right Hon. Doctor C. Addison, M.P., one of the leaders of the Labour party, stating what their aims are with regard to that marketing act. He says:
The powers that would require to be taken would be these:
(1)	Power to conduct purchases and control supply and distribution on national account, as far as necessary.
(2) Power to control the prices and the charges of distribution.
(3)	Power to ascertain costs and to fix fair prices.
And for the long term policy the powers that would be required are:
(1)	Power to plan land development.
(2)	Power to give effect to the plan by possessing.
(a)	Power to make the best and wisest use of the land;
(b)	Power over prices, including marketing, distribution and costs right down to the consumer; and
(c)	Ability to create the machinery for securing the progressive development of the plan.
Mr. Cole, who is a Labour authority in the matter, in an article entitled Planning International Trade, does not like the planned economy under capitalist conditions. He says:
What is doubtful is whether a planned economy introduced under capitalist conditions can possibly so establish itself in face of the powerful vested interests with which it will have to deal as to exercise the degree of control over the use of national resources necessary to afford a sure foundation for a system of internally planned production and trade.
And further:
Under such conditions national planning will lead, not to the regime of plenty which is now well within the world's grasp in view of its greatly expanded productive power, but to a perpetuation of scarcity, and to the shutting up of each developed country more and more behind a wall of economic nationalism, save to the extent to which the stronger countries are able by the methods of economic imperialism to force their way into the markets of the weaker and reduce the smaller countries *o the position of satellites.

Marketing Act-Mr. Lapoin.e
I should like to read more of Mr. Cole's article, but time does not permit.
Of course the socialist opposition there accepted with great cheerfulness all the new methods of dealing with the constitution, orders in council, minister, officials and boards being substituted for the authority of parliament. On May 29, 1932, in the report stage of the agricultural marketing bill, Sir Herbert Samuel moved an amendment to omit a clause providing that:
-the making of an order in pursuance of this section shall be conclusive evidence that the requirements of this act have been complied with.
The Labour party did not vote against it; they were delighted with the provision. What did Sir Stafford Cripps say? I quote:
This is an excellent precedent, which will be followed widely in the future, and seems to us in every way to be desired. We shall be delighted when on future occasions (as ministers) we have to draw the attention of hon. members opposite to the excellence of the precedent.
Again, on July 5, 1933, when an order made under the Import Duties Act was being discussed, Sir Stafford Cripps on behalf of the Labour party said:
We desire to put it upon record decisively that this is a mode of procedure which, if we get the opportunity, we shall adopt in an increasing measure. ... We hope we shall be able to utilize it for just such measures as the transference of the national wealth from one lot of people to another.
Nothing can better serve the purposes of those who desire to break away from the constitution and not be hampered by its provisions than this bill. I do not mean to suggest that all who favour the bill would favour the implications which I suggest. They certainly would protest against anything which would operate exclusively along the lines I have mentioned, but we are entering on the road which leads in that direction.
The most perfectly planned society is an army. All the fascist and communist countries have organized their planned economy on a military basis and along military lines-1'etat major, the staff which does the planning, captains and officers, then the officers who deal more directly with the rank and file, and then the rank and file which has to accept and submit to everything, as it is done in an army.

These planners have, of course, great confidence in the power of men to govern other men they think they are best suited to decide what is best for the individual 74726-233J
farmer or the individual industrialist. That is the state of mind necessary for the success of national planning. I quite admit it. But those who do not like this way of dealing with the people of a country cannot accept this. The rational method of dealing with the difficulties of the farmers at the present time I submit would be to try to increase the purchasing power of the consumers, to try to enact tariff and other economic legislation in such a way that people in the cities, towns and villages would be able to buy the products of the farmers and other producers instead of being forced to live on bread, potatoes and things of that kind, as thousands to-day are forced to do. In my view, to be at all effective a system like this must be universal and must be applied to all kinds of products. If, by reason of these regulations, the prices of some articles go higher while, other prices stay where they are or go lower, all the farmers will try to produce the articles selling at the higher prices, and there will be a glut on the market. That is unavoidable. You cannot force the consumer to buy where prices are higher; he will buy where prices are lower, and he will buy from the unregulated producer if he can get better prices there.
We are entering lightheartedly on the very difficult task of controlling thousands of small, unregulated farmers. As I said before, agriculture is a long range industry, in which you have to plan for years in advance. It is subject to changes and modifications of which the individual farmer is a better judge than any board sitting in Ottawa, Quebec or elsewhere. The economic planner, whether in Rqssia, Italy, Germany or elsewhere, seems to forget the human mind. There is a difference of mentality as between peoples and as between individuals. Russia can have its economic planning; Italy and Germany can have their plans, but I do not believe Canada will ever submit to any system which will make the state the master of the individual. I know the Quebec farmer, and I think the other farmers of Canada are much the same. The Quebec farmer will never submit to this system; he will never agree that his judgment should be subordinated to the judgment of any board however it may be organized. When the depression ends-and it will end- I submit that those planners will disappear like the night birds that are chased away by the sunshine. The Canadian farmers will remove this restriction on their liberty, and they will never accept what may be quite acceptable in a socialized state. Great institutions are rooted in the life and the habits of a nation and should not be subjected to

sudden changes. We cannot tear ourselves loose from our history and adopt unfamiliar and exotic arrangements which may be quite good in other countries and for other people. Historical, geographical and racial conditions in Canada will make those changes not serviceable to all the producers of our country in the same way. Paternalism is not what has made Canada what it is to-day. Regimentation is not what has made Canada a great success. Neither paternalism nor regimentation will make Canadians the great people they are destined to be. This bill represents an organization of bureaucracy, and if I have time I should like to quote a sentence or two from the May edition of a review entitled Canadian Business, which is not a political paper. Dealing with this bill this review states:
The oft repeated term "governor in council" in the bill leaves an indelible inference in the reader's mind and in making the act effective the government should remember that the control of commerce by such means tends to make trading uncertain and traders reluctant to make forward contracts.

I am told that I am at the end of my time, Mr. Speaker; perhaps the house does not regret it but I do, because I have something else to say. In conclusion, however, may I merely direct the attention of the house to the topsy-turvy policies of the government. In this bill they are trying to control nationally what is private business. In the Bank of Canada Act they control privately what is national and public business. Here we have absolutely two different standards, and in order to be logical I think the government should reverse the policies embodied in those two pieces of legislation.

My hon. friend stated that this bill will not help the producers, and that the farmer is the best judge of his own requirements and necessities. With the last point I agree; there is no doubt that the farmer is the best judge of his requirements and necessities. This is not a new matter; it is an old one and one which this house and the legislatures of this country have had under consideration for many years. We have dealt with it in a political way and our way affords a good illustration of political industry or government intervention in industry. It seems to me that the most sensible thing to have done would have been to analyze the causes of and the items which go to make up this gap. May I illustrate what I mean? There is the long haul, the short haul, the matter of cost of delivery; there is waste, insurance, conversion costs and, above all, the risks of the market. We have not entered into those matters. At the closing hour of the house this afternoon, the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) referred to this bill as a forward movement. The Solicitor General is a student and I fancy that he can find many quotations in Piers Plowman which will illustrate the argument which has been offered against price spreads. He is a lawyer and well versed in the history of the law and I have no doubt he will remember a case which we were told was rather famous, that of Rusby who was tried in 1800 for having made an excessive price spread advantage in the wheat market. He was fined and reprimanded by the court. Those who are familiar with the matter will remember that there were riots and the populace visited the home of Rusby and sought his life. Merchants were denounced as extortionists, particularly those in the wheat trade, but what happened? The merchants abstained from the market and the results were just the reverse of what was expected by the court and by the legislature.
I am very fond of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens)'-I hope he does not mind.
